mappings.note: The contrast with the spy of fiction is exactly the 'what the story implies about real espionage' half of LO-7, and the answer is built from Ausable's appearance and manner. Not C-E2.3-LO-3: no twist is involved.
Two retrievable facts -- Fowler is a writer, the thrill is the man with the pistol. Extraction.
The pass key and the main door: the true entry, stated in the text. Extraction; the invented entry is a separate item.
Ausable's claim that the balcony was the way in is the invention LO-2 names. Not LO-1, because the answer is a lie and the point is that it is one.
Sets Holmes, Poirot and Bond against Ausable, which is the story's comment on what espionage really looks like. Not LO-4: the comparison reaches outside the text.
Asks what makes the invented balcony convincing -- the suspense mechanism itself. Not LO-3, which is the fall rather than the set-up.
Whether the plan was prepared or improvised is a question about presence of mind. Not C-E2.3-LO-2: the device is not being analysed, the agent's quickness is.
Names presence of mind as the story's quality and asks for a parallel. LO-7 is the only outcome that carries it.

The textbook's follow-on drill -- kitchen fire, choking, sparks -- carries presence of mind out of the text entirely. LO-7 is the nearest honest citation; no outcome in this frame covers general safety discussion, and that is worth noting.
Names Robert Arthur. Extraction.
Completes the opening sentence with 'Ausable'. Extraction, not LO-4: no trait is weighed.
'Fat and sloppy' against three plausible alternatives is characterisation, and the item exists because the description defeats expectation.
Dictionary meaning of 'wheezily'. No LO in this frame reaches word-level vocabulary, so the competency is cited rather than forcing LO-1, which is about information.
The French hotel. Extraction.
The top floor. Extraction; the item does not ask why the height matters, so not C-E2.3-LO-3.
French and German. Extraction.
Boston. Extraction.
Twenty years ago. Extraction.
The American accent. Extraction.
Meaning of 'espionage'. Competency for the vocabulary reason above, although the word is the story's subject.
Fowler is a writer. Extraction.
His disappointment on meeting Ausable is the frame the whole story hangs on -- character. Pairs with the item asking how he feels at the end.
The sight of the automatic pistol. Extraction.
All three options are ways the real agent fails the fictional template -- the espionage-reality point. Not LO-1: the key is 'all of the above', so the item is about the pattern.
Meaning of 'slender'. Vocabulary, so the competency.
Ausable's version -- the balcony -- is the invention. The distractor 'passkey' is the truth, so the item turns on knowing the lie.
The door, not the balcony: the fact that makes Max's jump fatal. LO-3's 'what the reader was led to assume' is precisely what this item corrects.
The threat to complain to the management is part of the fabricated grievance that sells the balcony. Not LO-1: a detail of the lie, not of the story.
The pistol. Extraction.
Claiming the knock is the police is the second suspense device LO-2 names. Not LO-1: the claim is false.
The waiter, against the police Max was told to expect -- the assumption on which the ending depends.
Max jumping in the belief there was a balcony IS the twist. Not LO-2, which is the building of the belief rather than its consequence.
'Witty' as the defining trait. Character.
'With detailed description' names the technique by which the invention convinces. The LO-2 item in MCQ form.
Thrilled at the end, disappointed at the start: the pair completes Fowler's arc. Character.
Who fell from the top floor is the outcome of the twist.
Identifies the cooked-up story as the balcony. LO-2.
To take the missile report. Extraction of motive stated in the text.
The main door. Extraction of the true entry.
Max is a rival agent. Extraction.
The knock is named in LO-2 as one of the two suspense devices; this item asks who supplied it.
Fowler came to meet him. Extraction.
Boston again, in a different stem. Extraction.
Sixth and top floor. Extraction, treated the same as the earlier floor item for consistency.
The important paper. Extraction.
The pistol Max carried. Extraction.
'Invent and cook up situations that would confuse and unnerve his rival' is presence of mind named as a faculty. Not C-E2.3-LO-2: no single device is in question.
The key is the romantic picture from books and films, so the item is the espionage-reality contrast.
Physical appearance as characterisation. DEFECT: the option labels are printed (a) (b) (d) (d) -- there is no (c) and (d) appears twice.
'Never judge a book by its cover' plus 'outwits Max with his presence of mind' is LO-7 in both halves. Not LO-4: the proverb is about the gap between look and ability.
Henry the waiter exists in the plot only to knock at the right moment -- the device, not a character study.
Fowler's motive for seeking out a spy. Character; the text states it only obliquely, so not LO-1.
'Always one step ahead', with two instances: presence of mind evidenced. Not C-E2.3-LO-2, which would cover only the balcony instance.
The unintentional rescue by the knock. The suspense device seen from the waiter's side.
Awareness of the room's exits and of the waiter's timing is the groundwork of his quick thinking. LO-7.
The confidence rests on the six-storey drop the reader only now understands. The twist explained, so LO-3 rather than LO-2.
Pass key, and the missile report. Both stated. Extraction.
'Without using a weapon' is LO-7's own distinction between presence of mind and force.
The pretended anger at the management is the performance that makes the balcony credible. Not LO-1: the anger is staged.
Fowler's motive and his disillusion. Character, in the frame that opens the story.
Who was in the room and why. Both stated in the text. Extraction.
The core LO-2 question, here at three marks.
Asks the role of the non-existent balcony across the whole story, which is both the suspense it builds and the death it causes.
The paper that would affect the course of history. Extraction.
The elaborate detail -- the next apartment's balcony, the two rooms once being one -- is what makes the lie hold. LO-2.
'How was Max outwitted in the end' is the twist, and the means was wit rather than force.
Fowler's purpose and whether he got what he came for. Character, not LO-1, since the verdict is the student's.
Why he felt let down -- the gap between his imagined agent and the fat man before him. Character.
'Despite his unusual appearance, presence of mind' is LO-7 verbatim, asked at five marks, which is the extended form LO-3 measures.
All three alternative phrasings set intelligence against physical force. LO-7, at length.
Asks for the impression Ausable makes as an agent and how he consoles Fowler: character plus the espionage-reality point, as a long answer.
The knock turned to advantage, and then what it shows about him -- the device and the man. Not LO-3: the item stops before the fall.
'How did Ausable fool Max and get rid of him' is the twist plus the means. Not LO-2 alone, because the outcome is what is asked for.
An explicit character sketch of Fowler at five marks. Not C-E2.2-LO-7: Fowler does none of the outwitting.
Adds a moral judgement -- was it violence? -- to the presence-of-mind account, which is the 'what the story implies' side of LO-7.
A diary entry in Fowler's voice about his first impression: character, written at length. DEFECT: the stem says they met in a French music hall; in the story the meeting is at a gloomy French hotel.
'Disillusioned' is Fowler's character; 'take cheer' is Ausable promising the reality of the trade will be enough. Both halves, not LO-3.
How Max met his end, plus whether he deserves sympathy: the twist, evaluated, at five marks.
The printed extract is the opening description, and the sub-items ask about 'heart sank', an inference about Ausable, and the gloomy hotel -- character and setting, plus retrieval from the passage.
The extract is where the balcony lie is planted, and one sub-item asks outright whether the balcony existed. LO-2, with retrieval from the passage alongside.
